{"id":"62f9628b-51af-47c6-90aa-73ca529ea6bc","object":"chat.completion","created":1790516918,"model":"deepseek-flash","choices":[{"index":0,"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"{"support_claim_ids":["C5"]}","reasoning_content":"We need answer JSON only. Parent requirement has several elements: specific person and spouse; spouse up to 2019 no children from marriage; made foundational gift for construction of building that was part of larger complex. Claims:

C1 Kwon founded Smilegate...
C2 Kwon degree...
C3 Kwon as of June 2025 separated and 2 children.
C4 Ding Lei founded NetEase...
C5 Ding Lei degree; at time 2019 article, married but without children.

That matches part: spouse who up to 2019 had no children from marriage? Actually says "he was married but without children." It doesn't explicitly say spouse had no children from marriage? It says he was married but without children. Could support spouse no children from marriage? But parent requirement also requires person and spouse made foundational gift. C5 only supports marital/children status, not gift. Need substantive support for material part? The instruction: Counts as substantive support only when Claim itself establishes a material part of Parent Requirement with required entity, participant role, relation direction, object, temporal attachment, event/document binding, candidate branch. C5 establishes a material part? The parent requirement includes spouse had no children up to 2019. C5 does establish for Ding Lei that at 2019 he was married but without children. But does it establish spouse up to 2019 had no children from marriage? "married but without children" likely yes for that person. However, is it enough? The claim is about Ding Lei, one candidate. It supports the childlessness part. But parent requirement's main relation is "made foundational gift for construction..." No claim supports that. The question asks which current verified claims provide substantive support for one fixed Parent Requirement. If no claim directly supports gift, maybe none? But C5 could support a material part. The guideline: "A Claim counts as SUBSTANTIVE SUPPORT only when the Claim itself establishes a material part of the Parent Requirement with the required entity, participant role, relation direction, object, temporal attachment, event/document binding, and candidate branch." It says material part. C5 establishes married without children as of 2019 for Ding Lei. Is that a material part of R2? Yes: "spouse, who, up to 2019, had no children from the marriage" is a material part. But it doesn't mention spouse explicitly? "he was married but without children." It's about Ding Lei, so spouse exists. It doesn't say "from the marriage" but without children while married likely means no children from marriage? Hmm.

C3 says Kwon as of June 2025 separated and having 2 children, not relevant to up to 2019 no children. C1/C2/C4 no.

Could C4/C5 support identity of Ding Lei as founder of NetEase, which may be candidate for original question. But not R2 gift. The instructions say do not count useful for identifying candidate. So C4/C5 maybe not support R2 except C5 childlessness. But is C5 enough? Parent requirement requires "This person and their spouse, who, up to 2019, had no children from the marriage, made a foundational gift..." The claim C5 says Ding Lei married but without children at time 2019. It supports "spouse had no children up to 2019". But it doesn't link to gift. However, "material part" could be one condition. The examples: "a memorandum date does not establish the date of a different enclosed letter"; "person's nationality does not establish country..." They emphasize not just topically related. C5 is directly about marital/children status, one clause.

But maybe the intended answer: no claims provide substantive support because none mention foundational gift. Let's parse task: "You identify which current Verified Claims provide substantive evidentiary support for one fixed Parent Requirement." Parent requirement text is complete sentence. A claim counts as substantive support only when the Claim itself establishes a material part of the Parent Requirement with required entity, participant role, relation direction, object, temporal attachment, event/document binding, and candidate branch. It doesn't require establishing all. "material part" could be enough. But they also say Do NOT count merely because topically related, about same person, disease, university, useful for identifying candidate, generic background, compatible. C5 is not merely compatible; it's direct evidence of one element: Ding Lei was married without children at 2019. But is that a "material part" of R2? Yes, the spouse's childlessness up to 2019 is explicitly part of R2. However, the main point of R2 is "made a foundational gift for construction..." The childlessness is a relative clause describing spouse, not the core act. Does it need to establish "This person and spouse made gift"? Maybe the claim does not support the gift at all. The support_claim_ids should include claims that provide evidence for the Parent Requirement. If it only establishes an attribute of the person/spouse but not the gift, is that substantive support? The instruction says "material part" not necessarily central. But the examples: "a biography of a person does not establish that a target book cites them" (biography may establish person existed, but not target relation). Here, childlessness is part of target relation? It's a qualifier, not the target event. The target event is foundational gift. Without any claim about gift, the requirement is not supported.

Let's think of the original question: It asks "As of 2023, which university was this building a part of?" The chain: Person founder of company whose online video games division released a top-earning game in 2000-2010. Graduated from university founded 1930-1970. Person and spouse (no children up to 2019) made foundational gift for construction of a building part of larger complex. Building scheduled to open between 2018-2021, part of specific university. Which university as of 2023? This seems like Ding Lei and wife? They made gift for construction of building at University of Electronic Science and Technology? Wait, Ding Lei graduated from UESTC, founded NetEase, NetEase released Fantasy Westward Journey in 2003? Top-earning game. He and wife made gift for construction of a building? Maybe "Ding Lei and his wife donated to build a building at UESTC" something. The parent requirement R2 is about the gift. Current claims include C5: Ding Lei married but without children as of 2019. That matches the spouse no children. But no claim about the gift. C1/C2/C4 identify candidate. C5 also identifies marital status. But the task is to identify claims that support R2. It might be that C5 supports the childlessness part, so it's substantive support for R2. But if the parent requirement is the whole clause, maybe C5 is partial. The system might expect any claim that directly establishes any element of R2. The wording: "which current Verified Claims provide substantive evidentiary support for one fixed Parent Requirement." It doesn't say must support the entire requirement. "A Claim counts as SUBSTANTIVE SUPPORT only when the Claim itself establishes a material part of the Parent Requirement..." So yes, C5 establishes a material part (spouse had no children up to 2019). It has required entity (Ding Lei as person), participant role (married, no children), temporal attachment (2019). But does it establish "spouse" entity? It says he was married, so spouse exists. It doesn't name spouse. But parent requirement mentions "their spouse, who... had no children." C5 says "he was married but without children." That directly implies spouse had no children? At least no children in marriage. So C5 qualifies.

What about C3? Kwon as of 2025 separated and 2 children. This contradicts no children up to 2019? It doesn't mention up to 2019; as of 2025. Not support.

C4: Ding founded NetEase; no mention spouse/gift. Not support R2. C1,C2 no.

So likely answer includes C5. But need be careful: The parent requirement says "This person and their spouse ... made a foundational gift for the construction of a building that was part of a larger complex." C5 only says Ding Lei married but without children at 2019. It does not establish that he and spouse made gift. Is that "material part"? The phrase "who, up to 2019, had no children from the marriage" is a relative clause modifying spouse. It is a material part because it is part of the requirement. However, if we consider the core requirement is the gift, then no claim supports it. The task might be from a dataset where they want to see if a claim supports the requirement. The examples of non-support: "a memorandum date does not establish the date of a different enclosed letter"; "a person's nationality does not establish the country in which a case report was reported". These are similar: a claim about one attribute does not establish another relation. Here, C5 is about childlessness, which is a different attribute than the gift. But the parent requirement includes both childlessness and gift. Does C5 establish the childlessness part? Yes. But if the requirement is "made a foundational gift...", the childlessness is a condition. The examples say "knowing teammate names does not establish a same-country relation." That is a condition for something? They likely want to exclude claims that only support a qualifier but not the main relation. Hmm.

Let's examine the exact wording: "A Claim counts as SUBSTANTIVE SUPPORT only when the Claim itself establishes a material part of the Parent Requirement with the required entity, participant role, relation direction, object, temporal attachment, event/document binding, and candidate branch."

"Material part" could be any part. But then they say "with the required entity, participant role, relation direction, object, temporal attachment, event/document binding, and candidate branch." That suggests for the part it establishes, it must have all relevant dimensions. C5 establishes: entity Ding Lei; role person/spouse? temporal 2019; relation "married but without children" (no children from marriage). It doesn't have the object "foundational gift" or event "made gift". So it's only a part. The phrase "material part" might mean a component that is necessary for the requirement. The childlessness is necessary. So it should count.

But then would C4 count? It establishes Ding Lei founded NetEase, which is a candidate branch but not in R2. R2 doesn't mention company. So no.

C3: Kwon separated and 2 children as of 2025. Could it support "up to 2019 no children"? No, it says as of 2025 2 children, doesn't address up to 2019. Not support.

C5 also says Ding Lei earned degree, which is not R2. But the second half supports no children. So C5 contains a supporting statement. The claim ID is C5. Should we include C5? I lean yes, because the childlessness part is explicit in R2 and C5 directly states it for Ding Lei. The answer format expects a list of claim IDs. If no support, empty. The presence of C5 seems deliberately placed to match the "spouse no children up to 2019" condition. C4/C5 are about Ding Lei, who is the likely target person. C5 includes the exact temporal and childlessness detail from R2. That seems intended as substantive support for that part. So include C5.

But let's consider if C5 fully establishes "spouse ... had no children from the marriage". It says "he was married but without children." It doesn't say "from the marriage" but if he was married and without children, it implies no children from the marriage (unless he had children outside marriage, but typical interpretation). It also doesn't name spouse, but parent requirement only needs spouse relation. So yes.

What about C3? It says Kwon as of June 2025 separated and having 2 children. Could this be relevant to "spouse up to 2019 had no children"? No, because 2025. But could it support that up to 2019 he had no children? No, it says as of 2025 he has 2 children; children could have been born before 2019. So not support.

C1/C2/C4: no.

Thus answer: support_claim_ids: ["C5"].
